How a Top Law Firm Went From Standing Up to Trump to Bending the Knee
We’ve spent nearly a year trying to understand what led the law firm Paul Weiss to concede to the Trump administration and reach a deal over an executive order widely viewed as illegal.
On its face, the decision to settle without a fight looked like a stark pivot for Paul Weiss. The firm had a storied history of championing progressive causes and standing up to the government.
But our investigation found that the decision was the result of a wrenching reordering of power inside Paul Weiss that had been underway for years.
Brad Karp, then chairman, had hired a dealmaker named Scott Barshay to supercharge the firm’s corporate practice. Barshay worked to curtail social justice litigation, viewing it as bad for business.
Paul Weiss’s decision came at a pivotal moment in Trump’s retribution campaign, foreshadowing how his strong-arm tactics have ruptured an array of institutions and businesses.

Larry Ellison Bet It All on the A.I. Boom. Who Else Loses if He Fails?
My colleagues and I started reporting on Larry Ellison after he emerged from a quieter life on his private Hawaiian island to transform his company, Oracle, into an A.I. juggernaut.
His gamble initially seemed to pay off. In September, Oracle’s stock was soaring and Ellison briefly became the richest person in the world.
But Ellison’s big bet on A.I. was built on an astronomical amount of debt. And because the A.I. boom has been driving the U.S. economy, that has broad implications.
It’s a volatile moment. A crash could wipe out trillions in American wealth — far more than the dot-com crash in 2000 or even the 2008 financial crisis.
We interviewed dozens of people and reviewed financial documents to find out how Ellison, one of the biggest winners of the new A.I. economy, may become a cautionary tale.
